New Latinx destinations, adolescent friendship, and substance use: how migrant expansion inspires network revitalization
articles.abstract: Contrary to political rhetoric and stereotypes perpetuated by the media, Latinx migrants report lower rates of substance use than their native-born counterparts. These unanticipated benefits are not limited to migrants themselves but also strengthen the neighborhoods where they settle. Although social networks are frequently cited as a mechanism that could explain these patterns, it is unclear whether Latinx migrant expansion restructures our social networks. The current study addresses these gaps by offering the concept of network revitalization to describe how influxes of Latinx residents can reshape and reorient patterns of interaction. I evaluate the extent to which this social process occurs by applying stochastic actor-oriented models to fifty-three longitudinal adolescent friendship networks from rural Midwestern communities. Focusing on the coevolution of youth friendship and substance use, I compare the structural dynamics of networks embedded in new Latinx destinations to those in communities without growing Latinx populations. Results indicate that adolescents who use substances are less popular, less social, and less likely to form homogenous friendships when they attend school in new Latinx destinations versus non-destinations, though variations emerge across different substances. These findings suggest that network revitalization is an overlooked meso-level process that can help explain why migrant expansion enhances community well-being.

Financialization and Inequality in Child Education Investments
articles.authors: Nina Bandelj, Angelina Grigoryeva, Zaoying Ji
articles.abstract: Expenses to support children’s education have grown substantially over time. How do parents manage these costs? Although parental investment literature focuses on child expenditures, financialization of society has made widely available a range of financial instruments to parents, including earmarked savings plans, financial assets, and credit lines. Analyzing decades of the Survey of Consumer Finances data (1989–2022), this article reports on the significant growth in education savings, education debt, and financial assets under children’s names for families with children younger than 25 years. Importantly, although engagement in child education investment significantly increases over time for U.S. households, the kinds of financial instruments parents use vary substantially across income and race/ethnicity. High-income families, especially in the top 10 percent, are increasingly more likely to have pretax education savings and more financial assets under their children’s names. The opposite holds for Hispanic and Black households, and the latter are also more likely to be increasingly burdened by education debt for their children. Advancing the concepts of classed and racialized relational work, the authors suggest that the expectation of parents’ investment in their children’s education—given financialization, privatization, and rising tuition costs—is a driver of economic and racial/ethnic disparities among U.S. families.
